title: Encoding, framing and error control
subtitle: Turning bits into voltages, marking where frames start and end, and noticing — or fixing — the bit that got flipped.

sections.title: Line coding
sections.body: A wire carries voltages, so bits must be mapped to levels. NRZ-L holds a level for the whole bit; NRZ-I flips level for a 1. Both lose the clock on long runs of identical bits. Manchester puts a transition in the middle of every bit (low→high for 1, high→low for 0), so the receiver recovers the clock at the cost of double the signal rate — the code of classic 10 Mb/s Ethernet. Bipolar AMI sends 0 as no pulse and alternates + and − for 1s.

questions.prompt: Why does Manchester coding help the receiver?

choices.text: Every bit contains a mid-bit transition, so the clock can be recovered even from 000000.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: NRZ gives no edge during a long run of identical bits.

figures.caption: Figure 2.1.1 — NRZ-L, Manchester and AMI
figures.note: Step through: each code turns the same bits into a different waveform.

sections.title: Framing and byte stuffing
sections.body: The data link layer must tell the receiver where a frame starts and ends. A flag byte (HDLC uses 01111110) does it; to stop data that happens to contain the flag confusing the receiver, the sender inserts extra bits — bit stuffing: after five consecutive 1s in the data, insert a 0, which the receiver removes.

worked.why: After the first five 1s insert a 0 so the flag pattern 01111110 cannot appear inside the data.

questions.prompt: After how many consecutive 1s does HDLC insert a 0?

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Too late — the flag would already appear.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The flag has six 1s, so five in a row must be broken up.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: That is a byte count, not the rule.

sections.title: Error detection: parity, checksum, CRC
sections.body: A single parity bit catches any odd number of flipped bits but no even number. The checksum adds the words and sends the complement. The CRC treats the message as a polynomial and sends the remainder of dividing by an agreed generator G(x): the receiver divides the whole frame and accepts only a zero remainder. It catches all single-bit errors, all bursts up to the generator’s degree, and almost everything else. Dividing 1101011011 by 10011 gives the CRC 1110; the frame sent is 11010110111110.

questions.prompt: A CRC receiver divides the received frame by G(x). What does a non-zero remainder mean?

choices.text: The frame was corrupted in transit.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: A valid codeword is exactly divisible by the generator.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: Both sides agreed on it in advance.

figures.caption: Figure 3.2.1 — computing a CRC
figures.note: Long division with XOR — no carries.

figures.caption: Figure 3.2.2 — a corrupted frame
figures.note: Flip bit 3 in transit: the receiver’s remainder is not zero.

problems.prompt: Compute the CRC for data 1101011011 with generator 10011.
problems.answer: Append four zeros (degree of G) and divide with XOR; the remainder is 1110. The transmitted codeword is 11010110111110.

sections.title: Error correction: Hamming code
sections.body: Detection needs a retransmission; Hamming codes let the receiver correct a single-bit error itself. Parity bits sit at positions 1, 2, 4, 8…; parity bit p covers every position whose binary index contains p. After an error the failing parity checks, read as a binary number, give the position of the bad bit — the syndrome. Data 1011 encodes to 0110011; corrupt bit 5 and the syndrome reads 5.

worked.why: 4 data bits need r parity bits with 2ʳ ≥ 4 + r + 1.
So Hamming(7,4): 7 bits sent for 4 data bits.

questions.prompt: The Hamming syndrome of a received word is 101 in binary. Which bit is wrong?

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The syndrome is the position of the error.

figures.caption: Figure 3.3.1 — Hamming(7,4)
figures.note: Encode, corrupt a bit, locate it, fix it.

sections.title: PPP, HDLC and Ethernet
sections.body: HDLC and PPP frame point-to-point links with flags, an address/control field, a payload and a CRC. Ethernet (IEEE 802.3) frames carry destination and source MAC (6 bytes each), a type, 46–1500 bytes of data and a 4-byte CRC. The data link layer is split into LLC (flow and error control, protocol multiplexing) and MAC (who may transmit, and addressing).

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: That is the minimum frame size.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: That is the MTU; the minimum is 46 bytes.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
• Line coding maps bits to signals; Manchester embeds the clock.
  • Framing needs flags and bit stuffing.
  • CRC detects, Hamming corrects single errors.
